0.0.n: A polite way to address a group; さん adds respect.

0.2.n: A standard daytime greeting; the final は is pronounced わ.

0.4.n: Names the language taught by the speaker.

0.5.n: Links 日本語 to 先生, showing what subject the teacher teaches.

0.6.n: Here the speaker uses this job title to describe herself.

0.8.n: This is the speaker’s given name, written in hiragana.

0.9.n: A polite sentence ending used to identify herself; the Japanese leaves out I.

1.0.n: Sets the time for the introduction without needing a particle.

1.1.n: Attached to 今日, it suggests she has introduced songs on other days too.

1.2.n: Here it specifies the language of the song.

1.3.n: Links 日本語 to 歌 to describe a song sung in Japanese.

1.4.n: This is the thing the speaker will introduce.

1.5.n: Marks 歌 as what receives the action of 紹介します.

1.6.n: The polite form of 紹介する; here it announces what the speaker is about to present.

2.0.n: Names the season that brings this song to mind.

2.1.n: Marks 春 as what is mentioned in the expression と言えば, meaning speaking of.

2.2.n: The conditional form of 言う; together with と, it introduces something associated with the topic.

2.4.n: Must come directly before a noun, here 歌.

2.5.n: The sentence ends with this noun, leaving it is understood.

3.0.n: 桜 can name the trees or their flowers; here the focus is on their blooming.

3.2.n: The plain form directly describes 季節: the season when blossoms bloom.

3.3.n: The preceding 桜が咲く tells us which time of year is meant.

3.4.n: Marks 季節 as the state reached with なる.

3.5.n: With 季節に, it describes the arrival of that time of year.

3.6.n: After なる, it links a recurring seasonal change to what follows.

3.8.n: Points to the particular song the speaker has in mind.

3.9.n: Ending with this noun leaves the listener to infer that this song comes to mind.

4.0.n: 日本人 can refer to one person or many; here it refers to a group.

4.1.n: Links 日本人 to 多くの人, identifying the group those people belong to.

4.2.n: Combines with の before 人 to express a large number of people.

4.3.n: Connects 多く to 人 to form 多くの人.

4.4.n: Japanese nouns usually do not change form for plurals; 多く makes the plural sense clear.

4.5.n: Marks the people as those who know the song.

4.6.n: 知る in the ている form describes an existing state of knowledge, not an action currently happening.

4.7.n: Needs な when used directly before a noun.

4.8.n: Connects 有名 to 歌 so that the description modifies the song.

4.9.n: Both the preceding description about people knowing it and 有名な describe this noun.

4.10.n: Marks the entire described song as what the speaker will introduce.

4.11.n: 紹介 plus します forms a polite verb announcing the speaker’s next action.

5.0.n: With の, it identifies which work the title belongs to.

5.1.n: Links 歌 to タイトル, showing that the title belongs to the song.

5.2.n: An English loanword written in katakana.

5.3.n: Marks the song’s title as the topic; it is pronounced わ.

5.5.n: This is the song’s title, written in hiragana; the word itself means cherry blossoms.

0.lit: Everyone, hello. Japanese-language teacher, Noriko am.
0.tip: Japanese often leaves out I when the speaker’s identity is clear.

1.lit: Today too, a Japanese-language song will introduce.
1.tip: も after 今日 means today too, suggesting this is another song introduction.

2.lit: If speaking of spring, this song.
2.tip: と言えば is a common way to say speaking of and introduce an association.

3.lit: When it becomes the season when cherry blossoms bloom, this song.
3.tip: 桜が咲く comes before 季節 to describe it: the season when cherry blossoms bloom.

4.lit: Will introduce a famous song that many people among Japanese people know.
4.tip: Japanese puts the whole description of who knows the song before 歌, without a word like that.

5.lit: As for the song’s title, Sakura.
5.tip: The sentence leaves out です after the title, which is natural when simply naming something.
